findings.headline: H.R.30 sex-offense and domestic-violence immigration grounds
findings.compact: Foushee opposed passage of H.R.30 with those provisions; no preferred alternative is established. H.R.30 would add sex-offense and specified domestic-violence-related inadmissibility grounds, add conviction-based sex-offense deportability, and broaden the existing domestic-violence deportability definition.
detail: Foushee opposed passage of H.R.30 with those provisions; no preferred alternative is established.

The exact House-passed H.R.30 adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility for a person convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of a sex offense under 34 USC 20911(5), or a conspiracy to commit one. New 212(a)(2)(K) uses those same conviction/admission predicates for a crime of domestic violence (defined through 237(a)(2)(E)), stalking, child abuse/neglect/abandonment, or a crime violating the protective-order portion addressing credible threats, repeated harassment or bodily injury. The INA baseline makes these inadmissibility grounds relevant to visas and admission; the bill is not limited by its title to persons unlawfully present. It separately adds INA 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for conviction of a defined sex offense or conspiracy: admission of conduct alone is not the predicate in this new deportability clause. The existing 237(a)(2)(E)(i) after-admission conviction ground for domestic violence, stalking and child abuse/neglect/abandonment remains; its domestic-violence definition is expanded to include any crime constituting domestic violence under 34 USC 12291(a), regardless of whether the jurisdiction receives grants. Noncriminal behavior mentioned in the victim-services portion of that definition is not itself converted into a crime by this bill. The incorporated sex-offense definition covers criminal sexual-act/contact offenses, specified offenses against minors, listed federal/military offenses, and attempts/conspiracies, with its foreign-conviction fairness and consensual-conduct limitations. The latter exclude specified consensual adult conduct unless custodial authority exists, and specified conduct where the victim is at least 13 and the offender is not more than 4 years older. Some covered conduct already can trigger existing criminal inadmissibility or deportability grounds; these are additional grounds and a definition expansion, not the creation of all immigration consequences for these crimes. INA 101(a)(48) supplies the existing conviction framework, including specified withheld adjudications with a guilt/plea/facts predicate plus court-ordered punishment, penalty or restraint. H.R.30 references 20911(5), rather than expressly importing the separate 20911(8) juvenile-conviction definition. The bill leaves the 237(a)(7) discretionary battered-person waiver for specified domestic-violence/stalking/protective-order deportability grounds intact; that waiver is not written to cover the new sex-offense ground. Existing 212(d)(3) discretionary temporary nonimmigrant admission and 212(d)(13)/(14) T/U status waiver authorities remain within their own conditions. Existing 212(h) enumerates other criminal grounds and is not expanded to the newJ/K grounds. No universal waiver or automatic removal is established.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-01-16. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: The new inadmissibility clauses permit conviction or specified admissions. The new sex-offense deportability clause requires conviction. The existing domestic-violence/stalking/child-crime deportability clause retains its after-admission conviction condition; the existing protective-order clause separately depends on a court determination.

Sex-offense scope preserves 20911(5) foreign-conviction safeguards and consensual-conduct exclusions, including the at-least 13/not-more-than 4 years-older condition. The separate 20911(8) juvenile definition is not automatically treated as incorporated by the reference to(5); no individual juvenile-case conclusion is made.

The additional domestic-violence definition still requires a crime. Victim-service definitions that also describe noncriminal coercive conduct do not alone satisfy that predicate. Grant receipt is expressly irrelevant to the added definition.

The existing 237(a)(7) waiver requires a battered/extreme-cruelty victim who was not the primary perpetrator, and specified self-defense/protective-order/connected-crime conditions; the connected-crime route excludes serious bodily injury. The Attorney General retains credible-evidence discretion. This limited waiver does not extend automatically to new 237(a)(2)(G).

Existing inadmissibility exceptions and waivers retain their own enumerated scope. The 212(a)(2)(A) single-offense minor/petty-offense exceptions and 212(h) waiver are not stated as exceptions to newJ/K; retained 212(d)(3),T andU routes are discretionary and conditioned, rather than categorical relief.

This whole-bill House passage choice does not establish separate component preferences, wrongdoing, actual visa refusal, admission denial, deportation or enactment. The bill text addresses any alien meeting the grounds, rather than only unlawful presence suggested by its short title.

claim_source_map.passage: (5) Amie Zyla expansion of sex offense definition (A) Generally Except as limited by subparagraph (B) or (C), the term "sex offense" means— (i) a criminal offense that has an element involving a sexual act or sexual contact with another; (ii) a criminal offense that is a specified offense against a minor; (iii) a Federal offense (including an offense prosecuted under section 1152 or 1153 of title 18) under section 1591, or chapter 109A, 110 (other than section 2257, 2257A, or 2258), or 117, of title 18; (iv) a military offense specified by the Secretary of Defense under section 115(a)(8)(C)(i) of Public Law 105–119 (10 U.S.C. 951 note); or (v) an attempt or conspiracy to commit an offense described in clauses (i) through (iv). (B) Foreign convictions A foreign conviction is not a sex offense for the purposes of this subchapter if it was not obtained with sufficient safeguards for fundamental fairness and due process for the accused under guidelines or regulations established under section 20912 of this title. (C) Offenses involving consensual sexual conduct An offense involving consensual sexual conduct is not a sex offense for the purposes of this subchapter if the victim was an adult, unless the adult was under the custodial authority of the offender at the time of the offense, or if the victim was at least 13 years old and the offender was not more than 4 years older than the victim. (6) Criminal offense The term "criminal offense" means a State, local, tribal, foreign, or military offense (to the extent specified by the Secretary of Defense under section 115(a)(8)(C)(i) of Public Law 105–119 (10 U.S.C. 951 note)) or other criminal offense. (7) Expansion of definition of "specified offense against a minor" to include all offenses by child predators The term "specified offense against a minor" means an offense against a minor that involves any of the following: (A) An offense (unless committed by a parent or guardian) involving kidnapping. (B) An offense (unless committed by a parent or guardian) involving false imprisonment. (C) Solicitation to engage in sexual conduct. (D) Use in a sexual performance. (E) Solicitation to practice prostitution. (F) Video voyeurism as described in section 1801 of title 18. (G) Possession, production, or distribution of child pornography. (H) Criminal sexual conduct involving a minor, or the use of the Internet to facilitate or attempt such conduct. (I) Any conduct that by its nature is a sex offense against a minor. (8) Convicted as including certain juvenile adjudications The term "convicted" or a variant thereof, used with respect to a sex offense, includes adjudicated delinquent as a juvenile for that offense, but only if the offender is 14 years of age or older at the time of the offense and the offense adjudicated was comparable to or more severe than aggravated sexual abuse (as described in section 2241 of title 18), or was an attempt or conspiracy to commit such an offense.

findings.headline: S.5: expanding specified immigration detention and State enforcement litigation
findings.compact: Foushee opposed passage of S.5 with those provisions; no preferred alternative is established. S.5 would expand mandatory immigration custody and DHS detainers for the specified inadmissibility/offense combination (burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, assault of a law-enforcement officer, or any crime resulting in another person's death or serious bodily injury), and add harm-conditioned State suits over specified detention, release, parole and visa duties.
detail: Foushee opposed passage of S.5 with those provisions; no preferred alternative is established.

S.5 would extend the federal mandatory-custody category to the following offenses: burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, assault of a law-enforcement officer, or any crime resulting in another person's death or serious bodily injury. The listed property-offense terms, assault of a law-enforcement officer and serious bodily injury take the meanings assigned by the jurisdiction where the acts occurred. The exact bill adds an INA 236(c) mandatory-custody category requiring inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) together with a specified criminal predicate: being charged, arrested, convicted, admitting commission, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements. These inadmissibility categories concern presence without admission/parole or undesignated arrival, material immigration fraud/false citizenship claims, and specified entry-document defects, subject to their existing statutory qualifications. DHS must issue a detainer for a person meeting the new ground and, if the person is not otherwise detained by Federal, State or local officials, effectively and expeditiously take custody. The bill also gives a State attorney general or other authorized State officer standing, on alleged harm to the State or residents (including financial harm in excess of $100), to seek appropriate injunctive relief in district court over five specified federal matters: INA 235(b)(1)/(2) detention/removal requirements; INA 236 release, bond or parole decisions; the existing INA 243(d) visa-discontinuance requirement for countries denying or unreasonably delaying acceptance; violation of the existing INA 212(d)(5)(A) case-by-case urgent-humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole limits; and INA 241(a)(2) detention during the removal period. Courts must advance and expedite these cases to the greatest practicable extent. INA 236(e) removes its express release/grant shield while leaving the other printed discretionary-judgment/detention/revocation/denial restrictions, and INA 242(f)(1) receives an exception for the printed listed actions, while its separate final-removal-order injunction standard remains. These review changes do not establish a general right to enjoin every immigration action. The parole clause changes its named administering actor to the Secretary of Homeland Security. The baseline removal period is generally 90 days with specified starting/extension conditions; the bill adds litigation standing over its detention requirement rather than creating that period. The pre-existing narrow witness/cooperator-protection release exception remains, redesignated as INA 236(c)(4).
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-01-22. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: The listed property-offense terms, assault of a law-enforcement officer and serious bodily injury take the meanings assigned by the jurisdiction where the acts occurred.

The new custody ground requires both inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) and a listed offense predicate. Arrest or charge can suffice for the offense predicate; conviction is not required. Existing inadmissibility exceptions and waiver routes are not repealed, including specified battered-person/false-citizenship exceptions and document/fraud waivers.

The pre-existing INA 236(c) witness/cooperator-protection release exception is redesignated rather than repealed: release requires the specified protection necessity, no danger and likely appearance. Ordinary bond or parole is not substituted for that narrow exception.

State litigation requires alleged harm to the State or residents, including financial harm in excess of $100. Relief is appropriate injunctive relief and expedited handling to the greatest practicable extent; a filed suit or favorable judgment is not inferred.

Case-by-case humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole limits and the conditional visa-discontinuance duty for countries refusing or delaying acceptance already exist. The bill adds State enforcement standing and related review changes; it does not newly create those substantive baseline limits.

The visa-discontinuance duty arises after the statutory federal notification that a foreign country denies or unreasonably delays acceptance after a request. It covers immigrant visas, nonimmigrant visas, or both for the specified nationals/residents in that country, and lasts until the statutory acceptance notice. These conditions are retained, not newly imposed.

The existing INA 236(c)(1) when-released framework remains; the new DHS detainer clause separately requires expeditious custody when the person is not otherwise detained. No actual detention timing or individual outcome is inferred.

This is a whole-bill House passage choice. It does not establish separate component positions, guilt, actual detention/removal, a successful suit or enactment. The parallel House and Senate bills remain distinct proposal episodes; later enacted text does not replace either exact voting version.

Apprehension and detention of aliens (a) Arrest, detention, and release On a warrant issued by the Attorney General, an alien may be arrested and detained pending a decision on whether the alien is to be removed from the United States. Except as provided in subsection (c) and pending such decision, the Attorney General— (1) may continue to detain the arrested alien; and (2) may release the alien on— (A) bond of at least $1,500 with security approved by, and containing conditions prescribed by, the Attorney General; or (B) conditional parole; but (3) may not provide the alien with work authorization (including an "employment authorized" endorsement or other appropriate work permit), unless the alien is lawfully admitted for permanent residence or otherwise would (without regard to removal proceedings) be provided such authorization. (b) Revocation of bond or parole The Attorney General at any time may revoke a bond or parole authorized under subsection (a), rearrest the alien under the original warrant, and detain the alien. (c) Detention of criminal aliens (1) Custody The Attorney General shall take into custody any alien who— (A) is inadmissible by reason of having committed any offense covered in section 1182(a)(2) of this title, (B) is deportable by reason of having committed any offense covered in section 1227(a)(2)(A)(ii), (A)(iii), (B), (C), or (D) of this title, (C) is deportable under section 1227(a)(2)(A)(i) of this title on the basis of an offense for which the alien has been sentence 1 to a term of imprisonment of at least 1 year, or (D) is inadmissible under section 1182(a)(3)(B) of this title or deportable under section 1227(a)(4)(B) of this title, when the alien is released, without regard to whether the alien is released on parole, supervised release, or probation, and without regard to whether the alien may be arrested or imprisoned again for the same offense. (2) Release The Attorney General may release an alien described in paragraph (1) only if the Attorney General decides pursuant to section 3521 of title 18 that release of the alien from custody is necessary to provide protection to a witness, a potential witness, a person cooperating with an investigation into major criminal activity, or an immediate family member or close associate of a witness, potential witness, or person cooperating with such an investigation, and the alien satisfies the Attorney General that the alien will not pose a danger to the safety of other persons or of property and is likely to appear for any scheduled proceeding. A decision relating to such release shall take place in accordance with a procedure that considers the severity of the offense committed by the alien. (d) Identification of criminal aliens (1) The Attorney General shall devise and implement a system— (A) to make available, daily (on a 24-hour basis), to Federal, State, and local authorities the investigative resources of the Service to determine whether individuals arrested by such authorities for aggravated felonies are aliens; (B) to designate and train officers and employees of the Service to serve as a liaison to Federal, State, and local law enforcement and correctional agencies and courts with respect to the arrest, conviction, and release of any alien charged with an aggravated felony; and (C) which uses computer resources to maintain a current record of aliens who have been convicted of an aggravated felony, and indicates those who have been removed. (2) The record under paragraph (1)(C) shall be made available— (A) to inspectors at ports of entry and to border patrol agents at sector headquarters for purposes of immediate identification of any alien who was previously ordered removed and is seeking to reenter the United States, and (B) to officials of the Department of State for use in its automated visa lookout system. (3) Upon the request of the governor or chief executive officer of any State, the Service shall provide assistance to State courts in the identification of aliens unlawfully present in the United States pending criminal prosecution. (e) Judicial review The Attorney General's discretionary judgment regarding the application of this section shall not be subject to review. No court may set aside any action or decision by the Attorney General under this section regarding the detention or release of any alien or the grant, revocation, or denial of bond or parole.

(iii) Removal without further review if no credible fear of persecution (I) In general Subject to subclause (III), if the officer determines that an alien does not have a credible fear of persecution, the officer shall order the alien removed from the United States without further hearing or review. (II) Record of determination The officer shall prepare a written record of a determination under subclause (I). Such record shall include a summary of the material facts as stated by the applicant, such additional facts (if any) relied upon by the officer, and the officer's analysis of why, in the light of such facts, the alien has not established a credible fear of persecution. A copy of the officer's interview notes shall be attached to the written summary. (III) Review of determination The Attorney General shall provide by regulation and upon the alien's request for prompt review by an immigration judge of a determination under subclause (I) that the alien does not have a credible fear of persecution. Such review shall include an opportunity for the alien to be heard and questioned by the immigration judge, either in person or by telephonic or video connection. Review shall be concluded as expeditiously as possible, to the maximum extent practicable within 24 hours, but in no case later than 7 days after the date of the determination under subclause (I). (iv) Information about interviews The Attorney General shall provide information concerning the asylum interview described in this subparagraph to aliens who may be eligible. An alien who is eligible for such interview may consult with a person or persons of the alien's choosing prior to the interview or any review thereof, according to regulations prescribed by the Attorney General. Such consultation shall be at no expense to the Government and shall not unreasonably delay the process. (v) "Credible fear of persecution" defined For purposes of this subparagraph, the term "credible fear of persecution" means that there is a significant possibility, taking into account the credibility of the statements made by the alien in support of the alien's claim and such other facts as are known to the officer, that the alien could establish eligibility for asylum under section 1158 of this title. findings.headline: H.R.35 immigration consequences for specified border vehicle flight
findings.compact: Foushee opposed passage of H.R.35 with those provisions; no preferred alternative is established. H.R.35 would create a specified intentional vehicle-flight offense within 100 miles of the U.S. border and add conviction/admission-based inadmissibility, deportability and an immigration-relief bar including asylum.
detail: Foushee opposed passage of H.R.35 with those provisions; no preferred alternative is established.

The exact House-passed H.R.35 adds 18 USC 40B: operating a motor vehicle within 100 miles of the United States border while intentionally fleeing a pursuing U.S. Border Patrol agent acting under lawful authority, or a pursuing Federal/State/local officer actively assisting or under Border Patrol command. The ordinary penalty alternatives are imprisonment up to 2 years, a title 18 fine, or both; where serious bodily injury results the imprisonment alternative is 5–20 years, and where any person's death results it is 10 years to life, with fine-or-both alternatives retained in both cases. The bill adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility and 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for any alien convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of 40B(a). It also inserts 208A making a person meeting that same predicate ineligible for relief under the immigration laws, expressly including asylum under 208. Neither arrest alone nor merely being within 100 miles is the printed immigration predicate. Pre-existing 18 USC 758 already criminalizes vehicle flight/evasion from an immigration or other federal checkpoint followed by fleeing law-enforcement agents above the legal speed limit, with up-to 5 years/fine/both; existing 237(a)(2)(A)(iv) already makes a conviction for 758 deportable. H.R.35 creates a different officer/geography/intent predicate and additional immigration consequences, rather than the first-ever immigration checkpoint-flight offense or deportability ground. Unlike that existing deportability ground, the newG also accepts specified admissions. Existing INA 101(a)(48) conviction rules remain. The Attorney General, with the Secretary of Homeland Security, must report annually to both Judiciary Committees on violations, charged/apprehended/not-charged/not-apprehended counts, and penalties sought/imposed. A reporting duty is not evidence of actual violations, convictions or enforcement. The separate broad relief-bar clause is preserved as printed; it is not replaced by a blanket claim that existing narrow waivers guarantee relief, and no individual asylum or removal outcome is decided.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-02-13. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: The criminal predicate requires vehicle operation, within 100 miles of the U.S. border, intentional flight and the specified pursuing officer relationship/lawful Border Patrol authority. The bill does not state a legal-speed-limit or checkpoint element for new 40B; those are elements of the separate existing 758 offense.

The imprisonment ranges retain fine-or-both alternatives in the printed clauses. Serious bodily injury or death must result from commission of the offense for the corresponding enhanced alternative; actual harm or guilt is not established here.

New inadmissibility, deportability and relief ineligibility require conviction or the specified admissions of commission/essential acts. They do not follow merely from an arrest. The 208A relief bar expressly includes asylum; the candidate preserves its breadth without deciding individual relief/waiver interactions or actual deportation.

Existing high-speed checkpoint-flight law and its conviction-based deportability are retained, including the old 237(a)(2)(A)(vi) pardon exception for that ground. That enumerated exception is not automatically applied to newG. H.R.35 adds distinct grounds; newJ/G labels are evaluated within this exact proposal, rather than combined with same-numbered grounds in parallel pending bills.

This is a whole-bill House passage choice. It does not establish separate component preferences, enactment, actual enforcement, admission denial, asylum refusal or removal. The annual report provision requires reporting rather than creating actual enforcement outcomes.

claim_source_map.passage: SEC. 2. CRIMINAL PENALTIES FOR EVADING ARREST OR DETENTION. (a) In General.--Chapter 2 of title 18, United States Code, is amended by adding at the end the following: ``Sec. 40B. Evading arrest or detention while operating a motor vehicle ``(a) Offense.--A person commits an offense under this section by operating a motor vehicle within 100 miles of the United States border while intentionally fleeing from-- ``(1) a pursuing U.S. Border Patrol agent acting pursuant to lawful authority; or ``(2) any pursuing Federal, State, or local law enforcement officer who is actively assisting, or under the command of, U.S. Border Patrol. ``(b) Penalties.-- ``(1) In general.--Except as provided in paragraphs (2) and (3), any person who commits an offense described in subsection (a) shall be-- ``(A) imprisoned for a term of not more than 2 years; ``(B) fined under this title; or ``(C) subject to the penalties described in subparagraphs (A) and (B). ``(2) Serious bodily injury.--If serious bodily injury results from the commission of an offense described in subsection (a), the person committing such offense shall be-- ``(A) imprisoned for a term of not less than 5 years and not more than 20 years; ``(B) fined under this title; or ``(C) subject to the penalties described in subparagraphs (A) and (B). ``(3) Death.--If the death of any person results from the commission of an offense described in subsection (a), the person committing such offense shall be-- ``(A) imprisoned for a term of not less than 10 years and up to life; ``(B) fined under this title; or ``(C) subject to the penalties described in subparagraphs (A) and (B).''. (b) Clerical Amendment.--The analysis for chapter 2 of title 18, United States Code, is amended by adding at the end the following: ``40B. Evading arrest or detention while operating a motor vehicle.''.

claim_source_map.passage: SEC. 3. INADMISSIBILITY, DEPORTABILITY, AND INELIGIBILITY RELATED TO EVADING ARREST OR DETENTION WHILE OPERATING A MOTOR VEHICLE. (a) Inadmissibility.--Section 212(a)(2) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(2)) is amended by adding at the end the following: ``(J) Evading arrest or detention while operating a motor vehicle.--Any alien who has been convicted of, who admits having committed, or who admits committing acts which constitute the essential elements of a violation of section 40B(a) of title 18, United States Code, is inadmissible.''. (b) Deportability.--Section 237(a)(2) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1227(a)(2)) is amended by adding at the end the following: ``(G) Evading arrest or detention while operating a motor vehicle.--Any alien who has been convicted of, who admits having committed, or who admits committing acts which constitute the essential elements of a violation of section 40B(a) of title 18, United States Code, is deportable.''. (c) Ineligibility for Relief.--Chapter 2 of title II of the Immigration and Nationality Act is amended by inserting after section 208 the following: ``SEC. 208A. INELIGIBILITY FOR RELIEF RELATED TO EVADING ARREST OR DETENTION WHILE OPERATING A MOTOR VEHICLE. ``Any alien who has been convicted of, who admits having committed, or who admits committing acts which constitute the essential elements of a violation of section 40B(a) of title 18, United States Code, shall be ineligible for relief under the immigration laws, including asylum under section 208.''.

findings.headline: H.R.29: expanding specified immigration detention and State enforcement litigation
findings.compact: Foushee opposed passage of H.R.29 with those provisions; no preferred alternative is established. H.R.29 would expand mandatory immigration custody and DHS detainers for the specified inadmissibility/offense combination (burglary, theft, larceny or shoplifting), and add harm-conditioned State suits over specified detention, release, parole and visa duties.
detail: Foushee opposed passage of H.R.29 with those provisions; no preferred alternative is established.

H.R.29 would extend the federal mandatory-custody category to the following offenses: burglary, theft, larceny or shoplifting. The four listed property-offense terms take the meaning assigned by the jurisdiction where the acts occurred. The exact bill adds an INA 236(c) mandatory-custody category requiring inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) together with a specified criminal predicate: being charged, arrested, convicted, admitting commission, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements. These inadmissibility categories concern presence without admission/parole or undesignated arrival, material immigration fraud/false citizenship claims, and specified entry-document defects, subject to their existing statutory qualifications. DHS must issue a detainer for a person meeting the new ground and, if the person is not otherwise detained by Federal, State or local officials, effectively and expeditiously take custody. The bill also gives a State attorney general or other authorized State officer standing, on alleged harm to the State or residents (including financial harm in excess of $100), to seek appropriate injunctive relief in district court over five specified federal matters: INA 235(b)(1)/(2) detention/removal requirements; INA 236 release, bond or parole decisions; the existing INA 243(d) visa-discontinuance requirement for countries denying or unreasonably delaying acceptance; violation of the existing INA 212(d)(5)(A) case-by-case urgent-humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole limits; and INA 241(a)(2) detention during the removal period. Courts must advance and expedite these cases to the greatest practicable extent. INA 236(e) removes its express release/grant shield while leaving the other printed discretionary-judgment/detention/revocation/denial restrictions, and INA 242(f)(1) receives an exception for the printed listed actions, while its separate final-removal-order injunction standard remains. These review changes do not establish a general right to enjoin every immigration action. The parole clause changes its named administering actor to the Secretary of Homeland Security. The baseline removal period is generally 90 days with specified starting/extension conditions; the bill adds litigation standing over its detention requirement rather than creating that period. The pre-existing narrow witness/cooperator-protection release exception remains, redesignated as INA 236(c)(4).
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-01-07. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: The four listed property-offense terms take the meaning assigned by the jurisdiction where the acts occurred.

The new custody ground requires both inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) and a listed offense predicate. Arrest or charge can suffice for the offense predicate; conviction is not required. Existing inadmissibility exceptions and waiver routes are not repealed, including specified battered-person/false-citizenship exceptions and document/fraud waivers.

The pre-existing INA 236(c) witness/cooperator-protection release exception is redesignated rather than repealed: release requires the specified protection necessity, no danger and likely appearance. Ordinary bond or parole is not substituted for that narrow exception.

State litigation requires alleged harm to the State or residents, including financial harm in excess of $100. Relief is appropriate injunctive relief and expedited handling to the greatest practicable extent; a filed suit or favorable judgment is not inferred.

Case-by-case humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole limits and the conditional visa-discontinuance duty for countries refusing or delaying acceptance already exist. The bill adds State enforcement standing and related review changes; it does not newly create those substantive baseline limits.

The visa-discontinuance duty arises after the statutory federal notification that a foreign country denies or unreasonably delays acceptance after a request. It covers immigrant visas, nonimmigrant visas, or both for the specified nationals/residents in that country, and lasts until the statutory acceptance notice. These conditions are retained, not newly imposed.

The existing INA 236(c)(1) when-released framework remains; the new DHS detainer clause separately requires expeditious custody when the person is not otherwise detained. No actual detention timing or individual outcome is inferred.

This is a whole-bill House passage choice. It does not establish separate component positions, guilt, actual detention/removal, a successful suit or enactment. The parallel House and Senate bills remain distinct proposal episodes; later enacted text does not replace either exact voting version.

findings.headline: H.R.495 annual cross-border-tunnel strategic-plan reports
findings.compact: Foushee supported suspending the rules and passing H.R.495 to add annual implementation reports on the existing cross-border-tunnel strategic plan. H.R.495 would add annual CBP reports on implementation of the existing illicit cross-border-tunnel strategic plan after its initial report deadline; it does not newly establish that plan or authorize additional funding.
detail: Foushee supported suspending the rules and passing H.R.495 to add annual implementation reports on the existing cross-border-tunnel strategic plan.

The exact H.R.495 EH proposal adds “and annually thereafter” to Public Law 117-263 section 7134(a)(2), after “development of the strategic plan”. The Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection would therefore report on implementation of the existing counter illicit cross-border tunnel operations strategic plan not later than one year after its development and annually thereafter, to the House Homeland Security and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committees. The pre-existing 7134(a)(1) already requires the Commissioner, coordinating with the DHS Science and Technology Under Secretary and appropriate DHS officials, to develop the plan within 180 days of the 2022law. Its existing scope includes risk-based identification/breach/assessment/remediation criteria, technologies and community impacts, information sharing, Border Patrol sector indicators and technology/staffing needs. H.R.495 changes the reporting cadence, not those plan requirements. The separate 6 USC 257 annual report on discovered Mexico–U.S. tunnels and DHS prevention/investigation/prosecution needs already exists and is not the provision amended here. Existing 7134(b) authorized$1 million for each of fiscal 2023 and 2024 for plan development and remediation; H.R.495 neither extends that authorization nor supplies new appropriations. Membership follows direct border-tunnel operations reporting. Actual reporting, tunnel remediation, border outcomes or enactment are not established by the House suspension-and-passage vote.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-03-10. This does not establish enactment.

findings.headline: H.R.993 border-technology plan and innovation-team authority
findings.compact: Foushee supported suspending the rules and passing H.R.993 with its border-technology planning, innovation-team authority and procedures/reporting. H.R.993 would require a 180-day border-technology plan, authorize CBP innovation teams to research/adapt emerging commercial technologies, and require team procedures, metrics and reports; it does not require universal deployment or appropriate funds.
detail: Foushee supported suspending the rules and passing H.R.993 with its border-technology planning, innovation-team authority and procedures/reporting.

The exact H.R.993 EH proposal requires the DHS Secretary, acting through the CBP Commissioner and DHS Science and Technology Under Secretary, to submit a plan within 180 days of enactment to the House Homeland Security and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committees. The plan is to identify, integrate and deploy emerging/advanced technologies to enhance or address gaps in border-security operations. Its prescribed contents cover innovation-team use and composition, contributions and coordination, technologies from other agencies, procurement authorities and need for alternatives, scaling programs, program goals/timelines, border-community privacy/security impacts, replacement costs, research/private-sector coordination, metrics and listed aircraft/surveillance/inspection/tunnel/communications technologies. The bill gives the CBP Commissioner express authority to maintain one or more innovation teams to research and adapt new/emerging commercial technologies for border capability gaps and urgent mission needs, and assess potential outcomes including negative consequences where documented gaps are yet to be determined. It requires each maintained team to establish operating procedures, defined roles/partner relationships and transition protocols, plus strategic planning with costs, timeframes, metrics and performance parameters, including technology-transition rates. The Commissioner must report within 180 days and annually thereafter to the same committees on team procedures/plans, technologies piloted in the preceding fiscal year, success/gap determinations and status of transitioning successful technologies. This provides statutory authority and prescribed planning/reporting for maintaining teams; it does not establish that innovation teams or pilots first come into existence with this proposal. The technology list and planned deployment goals are not universal mandates to deploy every technology. No appropriation, universal pilot success or actual operational outcome is stated. Membership follows the express direct border-operations scope rather than DHS administration alone.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-03-10. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: The 180-day plan submission is assigned to the DHS Secretary through the CBP Commissioner and Science and Technology Under Secretary. The separate 180-day/annual team report is assigned to the Commissioner; both go to the two specified Homeland Security committees.

Team maintenance is authorized rather than mandatory creation of a particular number. Operating procedures/plans are required for maintained teams; their authority includes research/adaptation and assessing possible negative outcomes even before documented gaps are determined.

Plan contents include privacy/security impacts on border communities, procurement-authority analysis, cost estimates, timeframes and transition metrics. The list of technologies is not an order to deploy every technology, and reports on pilots are not proof of successful or universal deployment.

The bill supplies statutory team authority and planning/reporting requirements, not a claim that teams are historically new. It does not provide appropriations or establish actual spending, procurement, deployment, effectiveness or enactment.

This exact suspension-and-passage vote concerns the complete bill. It does not establish separate preferences about artificial intelligence, surveillance, individual technologies or any plan component.

claim_source_map.passage: (a) In General.--Not later than 180 days after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Secretary of Homeland Security, acting through the Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and the Under Secretary for Science and Technology of the Department of Homeland Security, shall submit to the Committee on Homeland Security of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs of the Senate a plan to identify, integrate, and deploy new, innovative, disruptive, or other emerging or advanced technologies that may incorporate artificial intelligence, machine- learning, automation, fiber-optic sensing technology, nanotechnology, optical and cognitive radar, modeling and simulation technology, hyperspectral and LIDAR sensors, imaging, identification, and categorization systems, or other emerging or advanced technologies, to enhance, or address capability gaps in, border security operations. findings.headline: H.R.23 conditional ICC-related immigration sanctions
findings.compact: Foushee opposed passage of H.R.23 with those provisions; no preferred alternative is established. H.R.23 would require conditional ICC-related sanctions, including visa/admission/parole and other INA-benefit restrictions and immediate entry-document revocation for designated foreign actors and specified immediate relatives, subject to waiver and termination provisions.
detail: Foushee opposed passage of H.R.23 with those provisions; no preferred alternative is established.

The exact House-passed H.R.23 requires the President, not later than 60 days after enactment and on an ongoing basis, to impose sanctions if the ICC is attempting to investigate, arrest, detain or prosecute a protected person. Covered foreign persons are those the President determines directly engage in or aid such an effort; materially assist, sponsor or provide specified support/goods/services for it; or are owned/controlled by, or currently act or purport to have acted for, a person directly engaging in it. For covered aliens, the bill makes them inadmissible, ineligible for visas or other entry documents, admission or parole, and any other INA benefit. Their visas/entry documents must be revoked regardless of issuance date, effective immediately and automatically canceling other valid visas/entry documents in their possession. The immigration sanctions also apply to each sanctioned foreign person's spouse, parent, sibling or adult child; the separate property-blocking requirement applies to the principal foreign persons described in 3(a)(1). Foreign person means someone other than the defined United States person, which includes U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, U.S.-organized entities and any person in the United States. The incorporated INA alien definition excludes U.S. citizens and nationals. Protected persons include any defined U.S. person unless the United States both formally consents to ICC jurisdiction and is a Rome Statute party. They also include foreign citizens or lawful residents of a NATO or designated major non-NATO ally that has not consented to ICC jurisdiction or is not a Rome Statute party. The listed military/government personnel are inclusive examples, not the entire protected class. The President may waive sanctions case by case for periods no longer than 90 days each on a reported vital-national-security determination before the waiver takes effect, including the specified detailed rationale and actions by the United States and ICC. The President may terminate sanctions on written certification that the ICC has ceased all covered efforts and permanently closed/withdrawn/ended/terminated them. Imposition also requires congressional briefing/written notice within 10 days. The package includes property blocking under existing IEEPA authorities and penalties, rescission of available ICC appropriations at enactment and a prospective ban on using appropriated funds for the ICC. Immigration membership follows the direct travel/admission/parole/benefit restrictions, not the foreign-affairs findings. These are proposed legislative requirements; existing general INA inadmissibility/temporary-admission authorities are not treated as newly created by this bill. Actual designation, visa revocation, sanctions, enforcement or enactment is not inferred.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-01-09. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: The trigger is an ICC attempt against a defined protected person plus the President's specified actor determination. It is not an unconditional travel ban on every ICC employee or foreign national. Protected-person conditions distinguish U.S. persons from citizens/lawful residents of defined allies.

Immediate relatives mean spouse, parent, sibling or adult child. Immigration sanctions extend to relatives who meet the INA alien definition; the principal-target foreign-person limitation is not assumed to exclude every lawful-permanent-resident relative. Property blocking in 3(b)(1) refers to the principal 3(a)(1) actors.
Visa/entry-document revocation is immediate and cancels other valid entry documents regardless of issuance date. No individual designation or actual entry refusal is established by a House vote.

Waivers are case by case, at most 90 days each, with a vital-national-security determination and a specified pre-effect congressional report. Termination requires written certification of both cessation and permanent ending of all protected-person efforts; ordinary general INA discretion is not substituted for this specific sanctions waiver.

This is whole-bill passage with property/funding provisions as well as immigration sanctions. It does not establish separate approval of each component, endorse the bill's findings, or establish actual spending, sanctioning, revocation or enactment.

claim_source_map.passage: SEC. 3. SANCTIONS WITH RESPECT TO THE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT. (a) In General.--Not later than 60 days after the date of enactment of this Act, and on an ongoing basis thereafter, if the International Criminal Court is engaging in any attempt to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute any protected person, the President shall impose-- (1) the sanctions described in subsection (b) with respect to any foreign person the President determines-- (A) has directly engaged in or otherwise aided any effort by the International Criminal Court to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute a protected person; (B) has materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of any effort by the International Criminal Court to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute a protected person; or (C) is owned or controlled by, or is currently acting or purports to have acted, directly or indirectly, for or on behalf of any person that directly engages in any effort by the International Criminal Court to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute a protected person; and (2) the sanctions described in subsection (b)(2) with respect to the immediate family members of each foreign person who is subject to sanctions pursuant to paragraph (1). (b) Sanctions Described.--The sanctions described in this subsection with respect to a foreign person described in subsection (a) are the following: (1) Property blocking.--The President shall exercise all of the powers granted by the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.) to the extent necessary to block and prohibit all transactions in all property and interests in property of any foreign person described in subsection (a)(1) if such property and interests in property are in the United States, come within the United States, or are or come within the possession or control of a United States person. (2) Aliens inadmissible for visas, admission, or parole.-- (A) Visas, admission, or parole.--In the case of an alien described in subsection (a), the alien is-- (i) inadmissible to the United States; (ii) ineligible to receive a visa or other documentation to enter the United States; and (iii) otherwise ineligible to be admitted or paroled into the United States or to receive any other benefit under the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq.). (B) Current visas revoked.-- (i) In general.--The visa or other entry documentation of an alien described in subparagraph (A) shall be revoked, regardless of when such visa or other entry documentation was issued. (ii) Immediate effect.--A revocation under clause (i) shall-- (I) take effect immediately; and (II) automatically cancel any other valid visa or entry documentation that is in the alien's possession.

claim_source_map.passage: (c) Implementation; Penalties.-- (1) Implementation.--The President may exercise all authorities provided under sections 203 and 205 of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1702 and 1704) to carry out this section. (2) Penalties.--A person that violates, attempts to violate, conspires to violate, or causes a violation of this section or any regulation, license, or order issued to carry out this section shall be subject to the penalties set forth in subsections (b) and (c) of section 206 of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1705) to the same extent as a person that commits an unlawful act described in subsection (a) of that section. (d) Notification to Congress.--Not later than 10 days after any imposition of sanctions pursuant to subsection (a), the President shall brief and provide written notification to the appropriate congressional committees regarding the imposition of sanctions that shall include-- (1) a description of the foreign person or persons subject to the imposition of such sanctions, including the foreign person's role at or relation to the International Criminal Court; (2) a description of any activity undertaken by such foreign person or persons in support of efforts to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute any protected person; and (3) the specific sanctions imposed on such foreign person or persons. (e) Waiver.-- (1) In general.--The President may, on a case-by-case basis and for periods not to exceed 90 days each, waive the application of sanctions imposed or maintained with respect to a foreign person under this section if the President submits to the appropriate congressional committees before the waiver is to take effect a report that contains a determination of the President that the waiver is vital to the national security interests of the United States. (2) Contents.--Each report required by paragraph (1) with respect to a waiver of the application of sanctions imposed or maintained with respect to a foreign person under this section, or the renewal of such a waiver, shall include-- (A) a specific and detailed rationale for the determination that the waiver is vital to the national security interests of the United States; (B) a description of the activity that resulted in the foreign person being subject to sanctions; (C) a detailed description and list of actions the United States has taken to stop the International Criminal Court from engaging in any effort to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute all protected persons; and (D) a detailed description and list of actions the International Criminal Court has taken to permanently close, withdraw, end, or otherwise terminate any preliminary examination, investigation, or any other effort to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute all protected persons. (3) Form.--Each report required by paragraph by paragraph (1) shall be submitted in unclassified form but may include a classified annex. (f) Special Rule.--The President may terminate the sanctions with respect to the foreign persons described in subsection (a) if the President certifies in writing to the appropriate congressional committees that the International Criminal Court-- (1) has ceased engaging in any effort to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute all protected persons; and (2) has permanently closed, withdrawn, ended, and otherwise terminated any preliminary examination, investigation, or any other effort by the International Criminal Court to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute all protected persons.

(a) In General.--Effective on the date of the enactment of this Act, any amounts appropriated for the International Criminal Court and available for obligation as of such date of enactment are hereby rescinded. (b) Prohibition on Future Appropriations.--On and after the date of the enactment of this Act, no appropriated funds may be used for the International Criminal Court. SEC. 5. DEFINITIONS. In this Act: (1) Admitted alien.--The terms ``admitted'' and ``alien'' have the meanings given those terms in section 101 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101). (2) Ally of the united states.--The term ``ally of the United States'' means-- (A) a government of a member country of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization; or (B) a government of a major non-NATO ally, as that term is defined by section 2013(7) of the American Service-Members' Protection Act (22 U.S.C. 7432(7)). (3) Appropriate congressional committees defined.--The term ``appropriate congressional committees'' means-- (A) the Committee on Foreign Affairs, the Committee on Financial Services, and the Committee on the Judiciary of the House of Representatives; and (B) the Committee on Foreign Relations the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, and the Committee on the Judiciary of the Senate. (4) Foreign person.--The term ``foreign person'' means a person that is not a United States person. (5) Immediate family member.--The term ``immediate family member'', with respect to a foreign person, means the spouse, parent, sibling, or adult child of the person. (6) International criminal court; rome statute.--The terms ``International Criminal Court'' and ``Rome Statute'' have the meaning given those terms in section 2013 of the American Service-Members' Protection Act (22 U.S.C. 7432). (7) Protected person.--The term ``protected person'' means-- (A) any United States person, unless the United States provides formal consent to International Criminal Court jurisdiction and is a state party to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, including-- (i) current or former members of the Armed Forces of the United States; (ii) current or former elected or appointed officials of the United States Government; and (iii) any other person currently or formerly employed by or working on behalf of the United States Government; (B) any foreign person that is a citizen or lawful resident of an ally of the United States that has not consented to International Criminal Court jurisdiction or is not a state party to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, including-- (i) current or former members of the Armed Forces of such ally of the United States; (ii) current or former elected or appointed government officials of such ally of the United States; and (iii) any other person currently or formerly employed by or working on behalf of such a government. (8) United states person.--The term ``United States person'' means-- (A) an individual who is a United States citizen or an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence to the United States; (B) an entity organized under the laws of the United States or any jurisdiction within the United States, including a foreign branch of such an entity; or (C) any person in the United States.

findings.headline: H.R.30 sex-offense and domestic-violence immigration grounds
findings.compact: Massie supported passage of H.R.30 with its additional inadmissibility and sex-offense deportability grounds and expanded domestic-violence definition. H.R.30 would add sex-offense and specified domestic-violence-related inadmissibility grounds, add conviction-based sex-offense deportability, and broaden the existing domestic-violence deportability definition.
detail: Massie supported passage of H.R.30 with its additional inadmissibility and sex-offense deportability grounds and expanded domestic-violence definition.

The exact House-passed H.R.30 adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility for a person convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of a sex offense under 34 USC 20911(5), or a conspiracy to commit one. New 212(a)(2)(K) uses those same conviction/admission predicates for a crime of domestic violence (defined through 237(a)(2)(E)), stalking, child abuse/neglect/abandonment, or a crime violating the protective-order portion addressing credible threats, repeated harassment or bodily injury. The INA baseline makes these inadmissibility grounds relevant to visas and admission; the bill is not limited by its title to persons unlawfully present. It separately adds INA 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for conviction of a defined sex offense or conspiracy: admission of conduct alone is not the predicate in this new deportability clause. The existing 237(a)(2)(E)(i) after-admission conviction ground for domestic violence, stalking and child abuse/neglect/abandonment remains; its domestic-violence definition is expanded to include any crime constituting domestic violence under 34 USC 12291(a), regardless of whether the jurisdiction receives grants. Noncriminal behavior mentioned in the victim-services portion of that definition is not itself converted into a crime by this bill. The incorporated sex-offense definition covers criminal sexual-act/contact offenses, specified offenses against minors, listed federal/military offenses, and attempts/conspiracies, with its foreign-conviction fairness and consensual-conduct limitations. The latter exclude specified consensual adult conduct unless custodial authority exists, and specified conduct where the victim is at least 13 and the offender is not more than 4 years older. Some covered conduct already can trigger existing criminal inadmissibility or deportability grounds; these are additional grounds and a definition expansion, not the creation of all immigration consequences for these crimes. INA 101(a)(48) supplies the existing conviction framework, including specified withheld adjudications with a guilt/plea/facts predicate plus court-ordered punishment, penalty or restraint. H.R.30 references 20911(5), rather than expressly importing the separate 20911(8) juvenile-conviction definition. The bill leaves the 237(a)(7) discretionary battered-person waiver for specified domestic-violence/stalking/protective-order deportability grounds intact; that waiver is not written to cover the new sex-offense ground. Existing 212(d)(3) discretionary temporary nonimmigrant admission and 212(d)(13)/(14) T/U status waiver authorities remain within their own conditions. Existing 212(h) enumerates other criminal grounds and is not expanded to the newJ/K grounds. No universal waiver or automatic removal is established.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-01-16. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: The new inadmissibility clauses permit conviction or specified admissions. The new sex-offense deportability clause requires conviction. The existing domestic-violence/stalking/child-crime deportability clause retains its after-admission conviction condition; the existing protective-order clause separately depends on a court determination.

Sex-offense scope preserves 20911(5) foreign-conviction safeguards and consensual-conduct exclusions, including the at-least 13/not-more-than 4 years-older condition. The separate 20911(8) juvenile definition is not automatically treated as incorporated by the reference to(5); no individual juvenile-case conclusion is made.

The additional domestic-violence definition still requires a crime. Victim-service definitions that also describe noncriminal coercive conduct do not alone satisfy that predicate. Grant receipt is expressly irrelevant to the added definition.

The existing 237(a)(7) waiver requires a battered/extreme-cruelty victim who was not the primary perpetrator, and specified self-defense/protective-order/connected-crime conditions; the connected-crime route excludes serious bodily injury. The Attorney General retains credible-evidence discretion. This limited waiver does not extend automatically to new 237(a)(2)(G).

Existing inadmissibility exceptions and waivers retain their own enumerated scope. The 212(a)(2)(A) single-offense minor/petty-offense exceptions and 212(h) waiver are not stated as exceptions to newJ/K; retained 212(d)(3),T andU routes are discretionary and conditioned, rather than categorical relief.

This whole-bill House passage choice does not establish separate component preferences, wrongdoing, actual visa refusal, admission denial, deportation or enactment. The bill text addresses any alien meeting the grounds, rather than only unlawful presence suggested by its short title.

findings.headline: S.5: expanding specified immigration detention and State enforcement litigation
findings.compact: Massie supported passage of S.5 with its specified custody/detainer expansion and State enforcement-standing provisions. S.5 would expand mandatory immigration custody and DHS detainers for the specified inadmissibility/offense combination (burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, assault of a law-enforcement officer, or any crime resulting in another person's death or serious bodily injury), and add harm-conditioned State suits over specified detention, release, parole and visa duties.
detail: Massie supported passage of S.5 with its specified custody/detainer expansion and State enforcement-standing provisions.

S.5 would extend the federal mandatory-custody category to the following offenses: burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, assault of a law-enforcement officer, or any crime resulting in another person's death or serious bodily injury. The listed property-offense terms, assault of a law-enforcement officer and serious bodily injury take the meanings assigned by the jurisdiction where the acts occurred. The exact bill adds an INA 236(c) mandatory-custody category requiring inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) together with a specified criminal predicate: being charged, arrested, convicted, admitting commission, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements. These inadmissibility categories concern presence without admission/parole or undesignated arrival, material immigration fraud/false citizenship claims, and specified entry-document defects, subject to their existing statutory qualifications. DHS must issue a detainer for a person meeting the new ground and, if the person is not otherwise detained by Federal, State or local officials, effectively and expeditiously take custody. The bill also gives a State attorney general or other authorized State officer standing, on alleged harm to the State or residents (including financial harm in excess of $100), to seek appropriate injunctive relief in district court over five specified federal matters: INA 235(b)(1)/(2) detention/removal requirements; INA 236 release, bond or parole decisions; the existing INA 243(d) visa-discontinuance requirement for countries denying or unreasonably delaying acceptance; violation of the existing INA 212(d)(5)(A) case-by-case urgent-humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole limits; and INA 241(a)(2) detention during the removal period. Courts must advance and expedite these cases to the greatest practicable extent. INA 236(e) removes its express release/grant shield while leaving the other printed discretionary-judgment/detention/revocation/denial restrictions, and INA 242(f)(1) receives an exception for the printed listed actions, while its separate final-removal-order injunction standard remains. These review changes do not establish a general right to enjoin every immigration action. The parole clause changes its named administering actor to the Secretary of Homeland Security. The baseline removal period is generally 90 days with specified starting/extension conditions; the bill adds litigation standing over its detention requirement rather than creating that period. The pre-existing narrow witness/cooperator-protection release exception remains, redesignated as INA 236(c)(4).
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-01-22. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: The listed property-offense terms, assault of a law-enforcement officer and serious bodily injury take the meanings assigned by the jurisdiction where the acts occurred.

The new custody ground requires both inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) and a listed offense predicate. Arrest or charge can suffice for the offense predicate; conviction is not required. Existing inadmissibility exceptions and waiver routes are not repealed, including specified battered-person/false-citizenship exceptions and document/fraud waivers.

The pre-existing INA 236(c) witness/cooperator-protection release exception is redesignated rather than repealed: release requires the specified protection necessity, no danger and likely appearance. Ordinary bond or parole is not substituted for that narrow exception.

State litigation requires alleged harm to the State or residents, including financial harm in excess of $100. Relief is appropriate injunctive relief and expedited handling to the greatest practicable extent; a filed suit or favorable judgment is not inferred.

Case-by-case humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole limits and the conditional visa-discontinuance duty for countries refusing or delaying acceptance already exist. The bill adds State enforcement standing and related review changes; it does not newly create those substantive baseline limits.

The visa-discontinuance duty arises after the statutory federal notification that a foreign country denies or unreasonably delays acceptance after a request. It covers immigrant visas, nonimmigrant visas, or both for the specified nationals/residents in that country, and lasts until the statutory acceptance notice. These conditions are retained, not newly imposed.

The existing INA 236(c)(1) when-released framework remains; the new DHS detainer clause separately requires expeditious custody when the person is not otherwise detained. No actual detention timing or individual outcome is inferred.

This is a whole-bill House passage choice. It does not establish separate component positions, guilt, actual detention/removal, a successful suit or enactment. The parallel House and Senate bills remain distinct proposal episodes; later enacted text does not replace either exact voting version.

findings.headline: H.R.35 immigration consequences for specified border vehicle flight
findings.compact: Massie supported passage of H.R.35 with its specified vehicle-flight offense and immigration inadmissibility, deportability and relief-bar provisions. H.R.35 would create a specified intentional vehicle-flight offense within 100 miles of the U.S. border and add conviction/admission-based inadmissibility, deportability and an immigration-relief bar including asylum.
detail: Massie supported passage of H.R.35 with its specified vehicle-flight offense and immigration inadmissibility, deportability and relief-bar provisions.

The exact House-passed H.R.35 adds 18 USC 40B: operating a motor vehicle within 100 miles of the United States border while intentionally fleeing a pursuing U.S. Border Patrol agent acting under lawful authority, or a pursuing Federal/State/local officer actively assisting or under Border Patrol command. The ordinary penalty alternatives are imprisonment up to 2 years, a title 18 fine, or both; where serious bodily injury results the imprisonment alternative is 5–20 years, and where any person's death results it is 10 years to life, with fine-or-both alternatives retained in both cases. The bill adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility and 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for any alien convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of 40B(a). It also inserts 208A making a person meeting that same predicate ineligible for relief under the immigration laws, expressly including asylum under 208. Neither arrest alone nor merely being within 100 miles is the printed immigration predicate. Pre-existing 18 USC 758 already criminalizes vehicle flight/evasion from an immigration or other federal checkpoint followed by fleeing law-enforcement agents above the legal speed limit, with up-to 5 years/fine/both; existing 237(a)(2)(A)(iv) already makes a conviction for 758 deportable. H.R.35 creates a different officer/geography/intent predicate and additional immigration consequences, rather than the first-ever immigration checkpoint-flight offense or deportability ground. Unlike that existing deportability ground, the newG also accepts specified admissions. Existing INA 101(a)(48) conviction rules remain. The Attorney General, with the Secretary of Homeland Security, must report annually to both Judiciary Committees on violations, charged/apprehended/not-charged/not-apprehended counts, and penalties sought/imposed. A reporting duty is not evidence of actual violations, convictions or enforcement. The separate broad relief-bar clause is preserved as printed; it is not replaced by a blanket claim that existing narrow waivers guarantee relief, and no individual asylum or removal outcome is decided.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-02-13. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: The criminal predicate requires vehicle operation, within 100 miles of the U.S. border, intentional flight and the specified pursuing officer relationship/lawful Border Patrol authority. The bill does not state a legal-speed-limit or checkpoint element for new 40B; those are elements of the separate existing 758 offense.

The imprisonment ranges retain fine-or-both alternatives in the printed clauses. Serious bodily injury or death must result from commission of the offense for the corresponding enhanced alternative; actual harm or guilt is not established here.

New inadmissibility, deportability and relief ineligibility require conviction or the specified admissions of commission/essential acts. They do not follow merely from an arrest. The 208A relief bar expressly includes asylum; the candidate preserves its breadth without deciding individual relief/waiver interactions or actual deportation.

Existing high-speed checkpoint-flight law and its conviction-based deportability are retained, including the old 237(a)(2)(A)(vi) pardon exception for that ground. That enumerated exception is not automatically applied to newG. H.R.35 adds distinct grounds; newJ/G labels are evaluated within this exact proposal, rather than combined with same-numbered grounds in parallel pending bills.

This is a whole-bill House passage choice. It does not establish separate component preferences, enactment, actual enforcement, admission denial, asylum refusal or removal. The annual report provision requires reporting rather than creating actual enforcement outcomes.

findings.headline: H.R.29: expanding specified immigration detention and State enforcement litigation
findings.compact: Massie supported passage of H.R.29 with its specified custody/detainer expansion and State enforcement-standing provisions. H.R.29 would expand mandatory immigration custody and DHS detainers for the specified inadmissibility/offense combination (burglary, theft, larceny or shoplifting), and add harm-conditioned State suits over specified detention, release, parole and visa duties.
detail: Massie supported passage of H.R.29 with its specified custody/detainer expansion and State enforcement-standing provisions.

H.R.29 would extend the federal mandatory-custody category to the following offenses: burglary, theft, larceny or shoplifting. The four listed property-offense terms take the meaning assigned by the jurisdiction where the acts occurred. The exact bill adds an INA 236(c) mandatory-custody category requiring inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) together with a specified criminal predicate: being charged, arrested, convicted, admitting commission, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements. These inadmissibility categories concern presence without admission/parole or undesignated arrival, material immigration fraud/false citizenship claims, and specified entry-document defects, subject to their existing statutory qualifications. DHS must issue a detainer for a person meeting the new ground and, if the person is not otherwise detained by Federal, State or local officials, effectively and expeditiously take custody. The bill also gives a State attorney general or other authorized State officer standing, on alleged harm to the State or residents (including financial harm in excess of $100), to seek appropriate injunctive relief in district court over five specified federal matters: INA 235(b)(1)/(2) detention/removal requirements; INA 236 release, bond or parole decisions; the existing INA 243(d) visa-discontinuance requirement for countries denying or unreasonably delaying acceptance; violation of the existing INA 212(d)(5)(A) case-by-case urgent-humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole limits; and INA 241(a)(2) detention during the removal period. Courts must advance and expedite these cases to the greatest practicable extent. INA 236(e) removes its express release/grant shield while leaving the other printed discretionary-judgment/detention/revocation/denial restrictions, and INA 242(f)(1) receives an exception for the printed listed actions, while its separate final-removal-order injunction standard remains. These review changes do not establish a general right to enjoin every immigration action. The parole clause changes its named administering actor to the Secretary of Homeland Security. The baseline removal period is generally 90 days with specified starting/extension conditions; the bill adds litigation standing over its detention requirement rather than creating that period. The pre-existing narrow witness/cooperator-protection release exception remains, redesignated as INA 236(c)(4).
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-01-07. This does not establish enactment.
qualifications_on_both_levels: The four listed property-offense terms take the meaning assigned by the jurisdiction where the acts occurred.

The new custody ground requires both inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) and a listed offense predicate. Arrest or charge can suffice for the offense predicate; conviction is not required. Existing inadmissibility exceptions and waiver routes are not repealed, including specified battered-person/false-citizenship exceptions and document/fraud waivers.

The pre-existing INA 236(c) witness/cooperator-protection release exception is redesignated rather than repealed: release requires the specified protection necessity, no danger and likely appearance. Ordinary bond or parole is not substituted for that narrow exception.

State litigation requires alleged harm to the State or residents, including financial harm in excess of $100. Relief is appropriate injunctive relief and expedited handling to the greatest practicable extent; a filed suit or favorable judgment is not inferred.

Case-by-case humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole limits and the conditional visa-discontinuance duty for countries refusing or delaying acceptance already exist. The bill adds State enforcement standing and related review changes; it does not newly create those substantive baseline limits.

The visa-discontinuance duty arises after the statutory federal notification that a foreign country denies or unreasonably delays acceptance after a request. It covers immigrant visas, nonimmigrant visas, or both for the specified nationals/residents in that country, and lasts until the statutory acceptance notice. These conditions are retained, not newly imposed.

The existing INA 236(c)(1) when-released framework remains; the new DHS detainer clause separately requires expeditious custody when the person is not otherwise detained. No actual detention timing or individual outcome is inferred.

This is a whole-bill House passage choice. It does not establish separate component positions, guilt, actual detention/removal, a successful suit or enactment. The parallel House and Senate bills remain distinct proposal episodes; later enacted text does not replace either exact voting version.

findings.headline: H.R.495 annual cross-border-tunnel strategic-plan reports
findings.compact: Massie supported suspending the rules and passing H.R.495 to add annual implementation reports on the existing cross-border-tunnel strategic plan. H.R.495 would add annual CBP reports on implementation of the existing illicit cross-border-tunnel strategic plan after its initial report deadline; it does not newly establish that plan or authorize additional funding.
detail: Massie supported suspending the rules and passing H.R.495 to add annual implementation reports on the existing cross-border-tunnel strategic plan.

The exact H.R.495 EH proposal adds “and annually thereafter” to Public Law 117-263 section 7134(a)(2), after “development of the strategic plan”. The Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection would therefore report on implementation of the existing counter illicit cross-border tunnel operations strategic plan not later than one year after its development and annually thereafter, to the House Homeland Security and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committees. The pre-existing 7134(a)(1) already requires the Commissioner, coordinating with the DHS Science and Technology Under Secretary and appropriate DHS officials, to develop the plan within 180 days of the 2022law. Its existing scope includes risk-based identification/breach/assessment/remediation criteria, technologies and community impacts, information sharing, Border Patrol sector indicators and technology/staffing needs. H.R.495 changes the reporting cadence, not those plan requirements. The separate 6 USC 257 annual report on discovered Mexico–U.S. tunnels and DHS prevention/investigation/prosecution needs already exists and is not the provision amended here. Existing 7134(b) authorized$1 million for each of fiscal 2023 and 2024 for plan development and remediation; H.R.495 neither extends that authorization nor supplies new appropriations. Membership follows direct border-tunnel operations reporting. Actual reporting, tunnel remediation, border outcomes or enactment are not established by the House suspension-and-passage vote.
The Clerk recorded the House result as 'Passed' on 2025-03-10. This does not establish enactment.
